newsitem.title: UK: Commodity regulators agree to step up supervision.
newsitem.headline: Commodity regulators agree to step up supervision.

text.p: Global regulators from 17 countries wound up a summit meeting in London on Tuesday agreeing a wide-ranging programme to strengthen supervision in many of the world's commodity markets.
But the regulatory agencies, meeting for the first time since the Sumitomo copper scandal earlier this year, did not propose any new measures.

"There was no decision on any new methods...we will look and see how new methods may be developed," Sir Andrew Large, chairman of the UK's Securities and Investment Board (SIB), told a news conference.
The meeting was co-hosted by the SIB, Britain's top regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI).

"It is important to have information about large (market) positions -- not only on futures, but also on the cash, physical and over-the-counter (OTC) markets. This has proved to be an invaluable tool in detecting manipulation," CFTC chairperson Brooksley Born said.
Large said the day and a half of talks had centred on utilising current regulatory powers as there was much more that could be done with the existing measures.

"In recognition of the increasing globalisation of these markets regulators have to come to a consensus...We have committed ourselves to information-sharing with respect to market disruption," Born added.
"We don't think things are too lax (at present), but we recognise that there is a need to address increased globalisation of these markets," she said.
The talks, which involved market overseers from Europe, South Africa, South America and Asia, including China, followed the Sumitomo affair, which rocked world metal markets.
The SIB, U.S. and Japanese regulators and fraud squads are currently investigating events surrounding the dismissal on June 14 of Yasuo Hamanaka, head copper trader for Japan's Sumitomo.

Sumitomo alleges that Hamanaka was a rogue trader who ran up losses worth $2.6 billion on unauthorised deals. Much of the business was carried out on the London Metal Exchange (LME), the world's largest metals market, which trades for immediate (cash) and forward delivery.

But Hamanaka also utilised physical markets, where commodities trade outside the control of exchanges, and the opaque OTC market, where futures and forward contracts change hands between traders, again outside market authorities' remit.
In London, regulators would not discuss any of the current investigations that might result in regulatory changes or criminal proceedings.
Large said the meeting was forward-looking, although nothing in this week's discussions would be inconsistent with the findings of the SIB review of the LME.
Instead, regulators agreed on a range of key measures in enhancing standards and best practice in contract design, market surveillance and information-sharing and cooperation.
The programmme of further work would increase understanding of existing arrangements and practices in different jurisdictions.
Large said two working parties had been set up and would start work immediately before reporting back at another commodity regulator summit to held next autumn in Japan.

The first working party would be chaired by the CFTC and would look at contract design, while the SIB and MITI would jointly chair the second group whose brief covered surveillance and information-sharing, Large said.
Born said the working party on contract design would survey various markets in other countries to see how individual contracts were handled and approved.
As the working parties proceeded, they would have contact with exchanges and the relevant industries.
"There is a mutual interest in making sure that improvements take place, both within the industry and in the markets," Large said.
Hidehiro Konno, Director-General of MITI, said commodity futures trade increasingly involved multiple markets and cross-border participants.
"We have a common interest in the global oversight of commodity markets," he said.
